caveats: All per-CFU values scale inversely with the assumed 1e8 CFU/mL assay inoculum, which is taken from the standard protocol and has NOT been confirmed against the Yamaguchi methods section. The agent-to-agent RATIOS, on which every conclusion in this study rests, are independent of it.
Values are derived from published abstracts, not digitized curves, so they are point estimates with no within-study dispersion.
A PBP-3 agent additionally carries a kill-independent filamentation yield (Y_filament ~ 1.5 fg/CFU/h), which is anchored on P. aeruginosa and is bounded above by Prins' E. coli result -- see Phase 3.
analysis1_yield_table.interpretation: Every agent in this table is BACTERICIDAL, and their yields still differ several-fold. The PBP-3 cephalosporins (ceftazidime, piperacillin) sit about 3.5-7x above the PBP-2 carbapenems at equivalent MICs, while the bactericidal aminoglycoside isepamicin sits at the same low end as the carbapenems (its value comes from Yamaguchi's absolute measurement, the carbapenems' from the revised ratio, so the two are not strictly commensurable). Yield therefore tracks the molecular target, not the bactericidal/bacteriostatic class -- which does not even vary across this table.
analysis1_yield_table.mechanism: The mechanism is PBP-3-SPECIFIC CELL-WALL DAMAGE, not filamentation as such. Trautmann 1998 settles this: ciprofloxacin induces filaments, with killing curves nearly identical to the beta-lactams, yet releases as little free LPS as the carbapenems -- so morphology does not predict release. Meropenem points the same way: it binds PBP-3 as well as PBP-2 and still releases little, so it is the DOMINANT PBP-3 specificity of the cephalosporins that matters. Filamentation is a marker of the relevant lesion, not its cause.

analysis2_dual_pathway.observation_to_explain: Jackson & Kropp 1992: sub-MIC ceftazidime released LPS in amounts MATCHING those at 1, 2 and 50x MIC, without significant lysis.
analysis2_dual_pathway.conclusion: A lysis-only model cannot reproduce that observation: with Y_filament = 0 the predicted sub-MIC release collapses, because there is almost no killing at 0.5x MIC to release anything. The kill-independent pathway is therefore REQUIRED by the P. aeruginosa data.
analysis2_dual_pathway.counter_evidence: Prins 1995 (E. coli, whole blood) found 0.5x MIC comparable to untreated with little agent separation, which the dual-pathway model does NOT reproduce. The two held-out sources conflict; Y_filament is plausibly organism-dependent and bounded above by Prins. Unresolved -- see PHASE3_VALIDATION.md section 6.

analysis3_matched_exposure.claim: At matched %fT>MIC the two agents achieve the same bacterial killing, and the PBP-3 agent imposes the higher danger-signal cost. The ratio is reported as a range over the measured 3.5-7x yield interval.

fT_pct.description: percent fT>MIC (the efficacy standard for beta-lactams)

analysis4_cost_index.interpretation: Across agents, the established efficacy indices rank inflammatory cost poorly or perversely, because they are agent-blind: two regimens with the same %fT>MIC differ several-fold in cost (3.6-7.6x) depending only on which agent delivers that exposure. Weighting cumulative killed biomass by the agent's yield recovers the ranking using only a standard PK/PD simulation plus a yield table, which is the practical proposal.

analysis5_divergence_map.interpretation: NO divergent step was found anywhere on the map: raising exposure never raised inflammatory cost. Two regimes explain it. ABOVE stasis, cost is nearly FLAT in exposure (a few percent across a 32-fold dose range), because cumulative killed biomass is bounded by the burden that is present -- you can only kill what is there, so how fast you kill it barely matters. BELOW stasis, therapy fails, the burden grows, and sustained kill-regrowth turnover makes cost explode by orders of magnitude. The practical reading is that there is no within-agent trade-off to exploit: under-dosing is bad for both objectives at once.
analysis5_divergence_map.hypothesis_amendment: This FALSIFIES the clause in DESIGN.md section 1 that 'the regimen that maximizes bacterial killing is not necessarily the one that minimizes host inflammatory injury' -- for regimens of a single agent above stasis, maximizing killing also minimizes inflammatory cost. The divergence the study is about lives BETWEEN agents at matched exposure, not between regimens of one agent. The hypothesis survives in its agent-comparison form and must be restated in that form.
analysis5_divergence_map.caveat: At the 20% fT>MIC cells the cytokine layer reaches occupancy ~0.82, i.e. it is saturating, so the magnitude of the failing-therapy cost is NOT interpretable there -- only its direction. See PHASE2_BUILD.md on the validity ceiling.

analysis6_predictions.prediction: At matched %fT>MIC against the same organism, ceftazidime and meropenem achieve indistinguishable bacterial killing but ceftazidime produces strictly greater danger-signal exposure and cytokine induction.
analysis6_predictions.quantitative: predicted cost ratio 4-8x (interval reflects the revised 3.5-7x yield range; see PHASE5B_AGENT_EFFECT.md)
analysis6_predictions.test: An in-vitro PK-simulation run of two matched-%fT>MIC regimens with serial free-LPS and whole-blood cytokine induction. This is a single experiment and it is the decisive one.
analysis6_predictions.falsified_if: cytokine induction is equal, or ordered the other way, at matched exposure and matched kill.

analysis6_predictions.prediction: %fT>MIC does not rank regimens by inflammatory cost across agents, whereas cumulative killed biomass weighted by agent yield does.
analysis6_predictions.quantitative: Spearman rho vs modelled cost: %fT>MIC -0.18, best candidate 'yield_weighted_kill' +1.00
analysis6_predictions.test: Rank a regimen library by each index and compare against measured cytokine induction.
analysis6_predictions.falsified_if: %fT>MIC ranks measured inflammatory cost as well as the yield-weighted index.

analysis6_predictions.prediction: The kill-independent (filamentation) pathway is activated by UNDER-EXPOSURE, not by reduced susceptibility as such. Reduced susceptibility matters only because, at a fixed dose, it causes under-exposure.
analysis6_predictions.quantitative: the filamentation share of release is a function of %fT>MIC alone: 0.39 at a 20% fT>MIC target and <=0.01 at 80%, and it is IDENTICAL at MIC x1 and MIC x64 when the dose is raised to hold %fT>MIC fixed
analysis6_predictions.test: Measure free LPS and cytokine induction for ceftazidime against isolates of graded MIC, once at a fixed dose and once at doses adjusted to hold %fT>MIC constant. The prediction is that the MIC effect disappears in the second arm.
analysis6_predictions.falsified_if: release per unit kill depends on the isolate's MIC even at matched %fT>MIC.
analysis6_predictions.note: This supersedes the Phase 1 statement, which was made at FIXED DOSE and so confounded susceptibility with exposure. The underlying numbers are unchanged; the attribution is corrected.

analysis6_predictions.prediction: Y_filament is organism-dependent: substantial in P. aeruginosa, small in E. coli.
analysis6_predictions.quantitative: the two held-out sources differ on this; the model reproduces Jackson & Kropp and contradicts Prins
analysis6_predictions.test: Repeat one sub-MIC release protocol on both organisms in one laboratory with one assay.
analysis6_predictions.falsified_if: both organisms behave the same, in which case one of the two published results is an assay artefact.

analysis6_predictions.prediction: No survival difference is predicted. The model predicts inflammatory exposure, and Simpson 2000 observed a significant endotoxin difference with identical mortality.
analysis6_predictions.quantitative: n/a -- this is a statement of scope
analysis6_predictions.falsified_if: n/a; recorded so the model is not over-read.
